question.prompt: On the same set of axes are drawn the graph of \(y=ax^2+bx+c\) and the graph of the equation obtained by replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) in the given equation. If \(b\ne0\) and \(c\ne0\) these two graphs intersect:

solutions.explanation:
Replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) leaves \(x^2\) unchanged and reverses the sign of the linear term. Thus the second graph has equation
\[
y=ax^2-bx+c.
\]
The two equations share their quadratic and constant terms, so subtracting will simplify the intersection condition.

At any intersection, the same coordinates must satisfy both equations. Therefore
\[
ax^2+bx+c=ax^2-bx+c,
\]
which simplifies to
\[
2bx=0.
\]
Since \(b\ne0\), division by \(2b\) gives \(x=0\). Substituting into either equation gives \(y=c\). The point \((0,c)\) satisfies both equations, and every intersection must have these coordinates, so it is the unique intersection.

Its zero \(x\)-coordinate places it on the \(y\)-axis. Since \(c\ne0\), it is neither the origin nor on the \(x\)-axis. Thus the graphs intersect exactly once, at \(\boxed{(0,c)}\), and the answer is \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
